paragraph_raw: For about a thousand years, the land walls of Constantinople were among the strongest defences in the world. Built in the fifth century under Emperor Theodosius II, they stretched for about six kilometres from the Sea of Marmara to the Golden Horn and consisted of three layers: a wide moat, a lower outer wall and a massive inner wall with nearly a hundred towers. Attackers who crossed the moat found themselves trapped between walls under fire from above. Many armies failed against them. Their end came in 1453, when Sultan Mehmed II besieged the city with enormous cannons that could batter the old stone walls in a way no earlier weapon could. After weeks of bombardment, Ottoman troops broke through on 29 May. Large sections of the walls still stand today and are part of a UNESCO World Heritage site.

paragraph_raw: In 1989, the American sociologist Ray Oldenburg introduced the idea of third places. The first place is home and the second is work; the third consists of informal public spaces such as cafes, barbershops, tea houses, pubs and parks, where people gather regularly simply to talk. Oldenburg argued that these places are essential to community life. They are open to everyone, cost little, and put people of different backgrounds on an equal footing, which helps build trust between neighbours. He warned that suburban design, long commutes and home entertainment were making third places disappear, leaving people more isolated. In many Turkish towns, the traditional tea house, or kahvehane, has long played exactly this role, especially for older men, though critics note that such spaces have often excluded women.

paragraph_raw: Many students now type notes on laptops, which lets them record almost everything a teacher says. paragraph_raw: When an aircraft flies faster than sound, about 343 metres per second at sea level, it overtakes the pressure waves it creates. paragraph_raw: Familial Mediterranean Fever is an inherited disease that is especially common among people of Turkish, Armenian, Arab and Jewish origin. Patients suffer repeated attacks of fever with pain in the stomach, chest or joints, usually lasting one to three days. Between attacks they feel completely well, which can delay diagnosis for years. A cheap daily drug, colchicine, prevents most attacks and also protects the kidneys from a serious long-term complication called amyloidosis.

paragraph_raw: Before conquering Constantinople, Mehmed II built Rumeli Fortress on the European shore of the Bosphorus in 1452. Remarkably, it was completed in only about four months. paragraph_raw: In some villages on Turkey's eastern Black Sea coast, bees feed on rhododendron flowers and produce a reddish, bitter honey known locally as deli bal, or 'mad honey'. The nectar contains natural toxins called grayanotoxins. In very small amounts, the honey is used as a traditional remedy, but a few spoonfuls too many can cause dizziness, a dangerously slow heartbeat and low blood pressure. The effect is not new: the Greek writer Xenophon described soldiers who, in 401 BC, fell ill after eating honey near Trabzon, although most recovered by the next day.

paragraph_raw: Dung beetles roll balls of dung away from crowded piles so that rivals cannot steal them. paragraph_raw: When preparing for exams, most students reread their notes and textbooks, because rereading feels productive. Research suggests this is one of the least effective methods. In a well-known 2006 experiment, students studied a short text and then either read it again or wrote down everything they could remember. Five minutes later, the rereaders did slightly better. A week later, however, the students who had practised recalling the text remembered far more. Interestingly, the rereaders had predicted they would do better. Psychologists call this the testing effect: struggling to retrieve information strengthens memory more than simply looking at it again.

paragraph_raw: In 1924, the world's largest light bulb makers, including Osram, Philips and General Electric, secretly formed a group known as the Phoebus cartel. Among other things, its members agreed to limit the life of ordinary bulbs to about 1,000 hours, at a time when many bulbs lasted longer. Companies that sold longer-lasting bulbs were fined. The cartel collapsed during the Second World War, but it is often cited as an early example of planned obsolescence, the practice of designing products to fail so that customers must buy again. paragraph_raw: Rabies is one of the deadliest diseases known: once symptoms such as fear of water or confusion appear, it is almost always fatal. Yet it is also highly preventable. The virus travels slowly along nerves from the bite towards the brain, which can take weeks or even months. This delay gives time for treatment. After a bite or scratch from a dog, cat or wild animal, the wound should be washed with soap and running water for about fifteen minutes, and the person should go to a health centre immediately for vaccination. Louis Pasteur first used this approach successfully in 1885, on a nine-year-old boy.

paragraph_raw: Turkish is an agglutinative language, which means it builds words by attaching a chain of suffixes to a root, each adding one piece of meaning. The root ev means 'house'. Adding -ler makes 'houses', -iniz makes 'your houses', and -den makes 'from your houses': evlerinizden. Where English needs three words, Turkish uses one. Because the order of suffixes follows strict rules, speakers can create very long words that are still perfectly clear. Learners from English-speaking countries often find this system difficult at first, but many later say it is beautifully logical, since there are few irregular forms to memorise.

paragraph_raw: In 2004, workers digging a station for the Marmaray rail tunnel in Istanbul's Yenikapi district struck something unexpected: the remains of the Harbour of Theodosius, a busy Byzantine port that had slowly filled with sediment and disappeared from view. The discoveries delayed the rail project considerably, but many now regard the excavation as one of the most important in the city's history.

paragraph_raw: A concussion is a mild brain injury caused when a blow to the head or body makes the brain move suddenly inside the skull. Contrary to popular belief, most concussions do not involve losing consciousness. Common signs include headache, confusion, blurred vision, sensitivity to light and feeling 'in a fog'. Some symptoms appear only hours later, so an athlete who seems fine at first may still be injured. One serious danger comes from a second blow before the brain has healed, which can cause severe swelling. For this reason, many sports now follow a simple rule: 'If in doubt, sit them out.' Players are expected to rest and return gradually, and researchers continue to study the long-term effects of repeated hits in sports such as American football and rugby.

paragraph_raw: Between roughly the fourteenth and nineteenth centuries, much of the Northern Hemisphere experienced a cooler period known as the Little Ice Age. Average temperatures fell by less than one degree Celsius, yet the effects were serious. Glaciers in the Alps advanced over farms and villages, and in London the River Thames froze hard enough for 'frost fairs' to be held on the ice, with stalls, games and even an elephant reportedly led across. Cold, wet summers ruined harvests and contributed to famine. Scientists point to several possible causes, including a series of large volcanic eruptions and a period of unusually low solar activity. The name is somewhat misleading, however: it was not a true ice age, and the cooling was uneven, with some regions hardly affected at all.

paragraph_raw: On the morning of 30 June 1908, a huge explosion shook the remote Tunguska region of Siberia. Witnesses dozens of kilometres away were knocked off their feet, and the blast flattened an estimated 80 million trees over more than 2,000 square kilometres. Most researchers now believe that an asteroid or comet fragment, perhaps fifty to sixty metres across, exploded in the air several kilometres above the ground. The heat and shock wave did the damage, while the object itself was largely destroyed. Because the region was almost empty of people, few deaths were recorded. Had a similar object exploded over a major city, the result could have been catastrophic.

paragraph_raw: After a major earthquake, rescuers sometimes pull out people who have been trapped under rubble for hours or days, only for them to collapse soon afterwards. One reason is crush syndrome. When muscles are squeezed for a long time, their cells break down and release substances such as potassium and a protein called myoglobin. While the person is trapped, these stay mostly in the crushed limb. Once the pressure is removed, they rush into the bloodstream, where high potassium can stop the heart and myoglobin can block the kidneys. For this reason, medical teams try to give fluids through a drip before or during the rescue, and survivors may need kidney dialysis for weeks. After the earthquakes in Turkey in 1999 and 2023, many survivors needed such treatment.

paragraph_raw: In 1971, the economist Thomas Schelling used coins on a chessboard to explore how neighbourhoods become divided. He placed two kinds of coins on the board and gave each a simple rule: a coin would move if fewer than a third of its neighbours were like itself. No coin wanted a neighbourhood entirely of its own kind; each was happy to be in a minority. Yet after a few rounds of moves, the board separated into large areas of one type. Schelling's point was striking: mild individual preferences can produce strong overall segregation that nobody actually intended.

paragraph_raw: The Black Sea is the largest body of water on Earth in which the deep layers contain almost no oxygen. Rivers such as the Danube pour fresh water into it, and this lighter water floats on top of the saltier, denser water that enters from the Mediterranean through the Bosphorus. Because the two layers hardly mix, oxygen from the air cannot reach the depths. Below about 150 to 200 metres, roughly ninety per cent of the sea's volume, almost nothing can live except certain bacteria, which produce poisonous hydrogen sulphide. This hostile environment has an unexpected benefit for historians. Without the worms and other organisms that normally eat wood, ancient shipwrecks on the seabed are astonishingly well preserved. In 2018, researchers announced the discovery of a Greek trading ship around 2,400 years old, still standing upright with its mast intact.

paragraph_raw: Thalassaemia is an inherited blood disorder in which the body produces too little healthy haemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen in red blood cells. People who inherit one faulty gene, called carriers, are usually healthy and may never know about it. But if two carriers have a child, there is a one-in-four chance in each pregnancy that the child will inherit two faulty genes and develop the serious form of the disease, which requires regular blood transfusions for life. The disorder is common around the Mediterranean, including parts of Turkey and Cyprus. In Cyprus, a screening programme introduced in the 1970s, which offered couples a simple blood test before marriage, led to a dramatic fall in the number of affected births. Turkey later introduced a similar premarital screening programme.

paragraph_raw: In the 1880s, two systems competed to supply electricity to American cities. Thomas Edison promoted direct current, or DC, which flows steadily in one direction. Nikola Tesla, backed by the businessman George Westinghouse, championed alternating current, or AC, which reverses direction many times a second. The key difference was transmission. DC lost much of its energy over long wires, so Edison's system needed a power station roughly every mile or two. AC could easily be raised to very high voltages with transformers, sent long distances with little loss, and then lowered again for safe use in homes. Edison fought back with a public campaign claiming AC was deadly. AC nevertheless won, and it still powers most grids today, although DC has returned for some very long undersea and underground cables.

paragraph_raw: Some nervousness before an exam is normal and can even help, sharpening attention and motivation. For some students, however, anxiety becomes so intense that it interferes with performance: their minds go blank, their hearts race, and they forget material they knew well the night before. Researchers believe that worry uses up working memory, the limited mental space we need to hold and process information while solving problems. Several simple strategies can help. In one study, students who spent ten minutes writing about their worries just before a test performed better than those who did not, perhaps because writing freed up mental space. Slow breathing can calm the body's alarm response, and reinterpreting a racing heart as excitement rather than fear may also improve results. Finally, regular practice with timed tests makes the real situation feel more familiar.

paragraph_raw: The mehter was the military band of the Ottoman army and is often described as one of the oldest military bands in the world. Its musicians played large drums, kettledrums, cymbals, trumpets and the zurna, a loud double-reed instrument. paragraph_raw: Why is the night sky dark? The question sounds childish, but it puzzled astronomers for centuries. If the universe were infinite, unchanging and evenly filled with stars, then every line of sight from Earth would eventually end on the surface of a star. The whole sky would then shine as brightly as the Sun, day and night. This puzzle is known as Olbers' paradox, after the German astronomer Heinrich Olbers, who discussed it in 1823. The modern answer has two main parts. First, the universe has a finite age, about 13.8 billion years, so light from very distant stars has not yet had time to reach us. Second, the universe is expanding, which stretches the light of distant galaxies to longer wavelengths that our eyes cannot see. The darkness of the night is therefore a clue about the history of the universe.

paragraph_raw: In the mid-nineteenth century, surgery was often a death sentence, not because of the operation itself but because of what followed. Wounds frequently became infected, and in some hospitals nearly half of patients who had limbs amputated died. Many doctors blamed 'bad air'. The British surgeon Joseph Lister took a different view after reading Louis Pasteur's work showing that tiny living organisms cause decay. If germs caused rotting, Lister reasoned, they might also cause wound infections. In 1867 he began cleaning wounds, instruments and dressings with carbolic acid, a chemical already used to treat sewage. The death rate among his amputation patients fell sharply. Many surgeons at first mocked his methods, which were unpleasant and time-consuming, but within a few decades antiseptic and then sterile surgery became standard.

paragraph_raw: Around 1274 BC, the armies of Egypt and the Hittite Empire met at Kadesh, in what is now Syria, in one of the largest chariot battles in history. Both sides later claimed victory. About fifteen years afterwards, the pharaoh Ramesses II and the Hittite king Hattusili III agreed a peace treaty, promising not to attack each other and to help each other against enemies. It is often described as the oldest surviving peace treaty. Copies were found both in Egypt, carved on temple walls, and at Hattusa, the Hittite capital near Corum in central Turkey, where archaeologists discovered clay tablets written in Akkadian, the diplomatic language of the time. A copy of the treaty is displayed at the United Nations headquarters in New York as a symbol of peaceful diplomacy.

paragraph_raw: Japan has one of the oldest populations in the world. Nearly thirty per cent of its people are aged sixty-five or over, and the country has more than ninety thousand people aged one hundred or older. This is partly a success story: Japanese people enjoy some of the longest lives on Earth, thanks to good healthcare and diet. But it also creates serious challenges. Because the birth rate has been low for decades, the working-age population is shrinking, while the number of people needing pensions and care keeps rising. Rural villages have emptied as young people move to cities, and some schools have closed for lack of children. The government has responded with measures ranging from support for parents to robots in care homes. Many other countries, including Turkey, are watching closely, as their own populations are ageing too.

paragraph_raw: In a country like Turkey, where large earthquakes are a constant risk, preparing before disaster strikes can save lives. Experts recommend that every household keep an emergency bag in an easy-to-reach place, such as near the front door. It should contain enough drinking water for at least three days, food that does not need cooking, a torch with spare batteries, a whistle, a basic first-aid kit, copies of important documents and any regular medicines. The whistle may seem a small detail, but a person trapped under rubble can use it to signal to rescuers without exhausting themselves by shouting. Families are also advised to agree on a meeting point in case they are separated, since phone networks often fail or become overloaded after a major earthquake. Finally, heavy furniture such as bookcases should be fixed to the walls.

paragraph_raw: The heart has its own natural pacemaker, a small cluster of cells that sends regular electrical signals telling the heart muscle when to contract. Modern pacemakers are smaller than a matchbox and can last for many years.

paragraph_raw: Many successful people secretly feel that they do not deserve their achievements and fear that one day they will be 'found out'. paragraph_raw: Many teachers and students believe that each person learns best in their preferred 'learning style', such as visual, auditory or kinaesthetic, and that teaching should be matched to it. paragraph_raw: The dodo was a large, flightless bird that lived only on the island of Mauritius in the Indian Ocean. With no natural predators on the island, it had no reason to fear other animals and nested on the ground. When Dutch sailors arrived in the late sixteenth century, they found the birds easy to catch. Yet hunting was probably not the main cause of the dodo's extinction. The sailors also brought rats, pigs, monkeys and other animals, which destroyed nests and ate the eggs. Within less than a century of human arrival, the last reliable sightings had been recorded, and the dodo was gone. Because so little was preserved, much of what we believe about its appearance comes from paintings, some of which may have shown overfed birds kept in captivity. Its story has become a powerful symbol of how quickly humans can cause extinction.

paragraph_raw: In 1953, James Watson and Francis Crick published a short paper proposing that DNA has the shape of a double helix, two strands twisted around each other like a spiral staircase. The model explained how genetic information could be copied: each strand could serve as a template for a new partner. Their discovery relied heavily on the work of Rosalind Franklin, a chemist at King's College London, whose X-ray images of DNA, especially one known as Photograph 51, revealed its helical shape. Watson and Crick saw some of her data without her knowledge. Franklin died of cancer in 1958, aged thirty-seven. When the Nobel Prize was awarded in 1962 to Watson, Crick and Maurice Wilkins, she could not be included, since the prize is not given after death. Today she is widely recognised as a key figure in one of the greatest discoveries of the twentieth century.

paragraph_raw: In 1854, a severe outbreak of cholera killed more than five hundred people in about ten days in the Soho district of London. At the time, most doctors believed that cholera spread through 'bad air'. The physician John Snow suspected contaminated water instead. He interviewed local families and marked each death on a map. The deaths clustered around a public water pump on Broad Street. Snow also noticed revealing exceptions: workers at a nearby brewery, who drank beer rather than water, were largely spared, while a woman who lived far away but had water from the pump delivered because she liked its taste died of the disease. Snow persuaded local officials to remove the pump's handle, and the outbreak, which was already declining, ended. His map is now regarded as a founding moment of epidemiology.

paragraph_raw: On the summit of Mount Nemrut in south-eastern Turkey, more than two thousand metres above sea level, stand the remains of a monument built in the first century BC by Antiochus I, king of Commagene. paragraph_raw: Economists use the term 'public good' for something that everyone can benefit from and that no one can easily be stopped from using. Street lighting and national defence are common examples. Such goods create a problem: because people can enjoy them without paying, private businesses may have little reason to provide them, so governments usually step in. For decades, the lighthouse was the classic textbook example, since a ship's captain can see its light without paying anything. In 1974, however, the economist Ronald Coase pointed out that many lighthouses in Britain had in fact been built and run privately, funded by fees collected from ships when they arrived in port. His point was not that governments are never needed, but that people can be more creative in solving such problems than theory suggests.

paragraph_raw: Many songbirds are not born knowing their songs; they learn them from adult birds, much as human children learn to speak. Young birds listen during a sensitive period early in life and then practise, producing imperfect attempts that researchers compare to babbling. As a result, birds of the same species in different areas can develop local dialects. White-crowned sparrows in California, for example, sing noticeably different versions of their song only a few kilometres apart.

paragraph_raw: Confirmation bias is the tendency to notice, remember and trust information that supports what we already believe, while ignoring evidence against it. paragraph_raw: Everyone yawns, from newborn babies to the elderly, and so do many animals, yet scientists still do not fully agree on why. One older idea, that yawning raises oxygen levels in the blood, has not been supported by experiments: breathing extra oxygen does not reduce yawning. A more recent theory suggests that yawning helps cool the brain, since the deep breath and stretching of the jaw increase blood flow and bring in cooler air. Supporting this, people yawn less often when the air is very hot. Yawning is also contagious: seeing, hearing or even reading about yawning can trigger it, and some researchers link this to social bonding.

paragraph_raw: For people who are short-sighted, the eye focuses light in front of the retina instead of on it, making distant objects blurry. paragraph_raw: Many people have heard that grief follows five fixed stages: denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance. The model comes from the psychiatrist Elisabeth Kubler-Ross, who described it in 1969, originally based on her work with dying patients rather than with the bereaved. Many grieving people also experience moments of laughter and relief, which they may wrongly feel guilty about. Experts now emphasise that there is no single correct way to grieve, and that most people gradually adapt with the support of others.

paragraph_raw: Desert locusts are usually shy, solitary insects, a type of grasshopper that avoids others of its kind. But when heavy rains produce plenty of vegetation and numbers rise, crowding triggers a dramatic change. Repeated contact with other locusts, especially touching on the back legs, causes a rise in the brain chemical serotonin. Within hours, the insects become attracted to each other and more active; over generations they even change colour and shape. paragraph_raw: Asthma is a long-term condition in which the airways of the lungs become inflamed and sensitive. When triggered by things such as dust, pollen, cold air or exercise, the muscles around the airways tighten and the lining swells, making it hard to breathe and causing wheezing and coughing. Most patients use two kinds of inhaler. A 'reliever', often blue, relaxes the airway muscles within minutes and is used during an attack. A 'preventer' contains a low dose of steroid that reduces inflammation over time; it must be used every day, even when the person feels well, and its benefits build up gradually. A common problem is that patients stop using their preventer once symptoms improve, and then rely too heavily on the reliever, which can be a sign that their asthma is poorly controlled.

paragraph_raw: In many countries, a large share of all antibiotics is given not to people but to farm animals. For decades, farmers added small doses to animal feed, not only to treat illness but to make animals grow faster and to prevent disease in crowded conditions. When bacteria are regularly exposed to low doses of antibiotics, those that happen to survive multiply, and resistant strains can then spread to people through food, water or direct contact with animals. Critics argue that further reductions are needed, while some farmers point out that better hygiene, vaccination and more space for animals can reduce the need for these drugs.

paragraph_raw: The Yoruks are Turkish-speaking nomadic communities of Anatolia whose way of life is built around seasonal migration. Traditionally, families spent the winter on the warm coastal plains of the Mediterranean and Aegean regions and moved their flocks of goats and sheep up to the cool mountain pastures, known as yayla, in late spring. The tents were well suited to this life: the woven hair swells when wet, keeping out rain, and lets air pass in dry heat. paragraph_raw: Moral hazard describes a situation in which people take greater risks because they do not bear the full cost if things go wrong. The term comes from the insurance industry. paragraph_raw: At the ends of our chromosomes are protective caps called telomeres, often compared to the plastic tips on shoelaces that stop them from fraying. paragraph_raw: In 1869, the Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev published a table that arranged the sixty or so known chemical elements in order of their atomic weight, grouping together those with similar properties. Others had noticed patterns before, but Mendeleev took a bold step. Where an element seemed to be missing, he left a gap rather than forcing the pattern, and he predicted the properties of the undiscovered elements that should fill them. For one, which he called eka-aluminium, he forecast its weight and density. When gallium was discovered in 1875, its properties closely matched his predictions. Gallium indeed melts at about thirty degrees Celsius, low enough to melt in a person's hand. Such successful predictions convinced many sceptical scientists, and his table became the foundation of modern chemistry.

paragraph_raw: In 1937, the Turkish dermatologist Hulusi Behcet described a disease he had observed in several patients over many years: repeated painful mouth ulcers, genital ulcers and inflammation of the eye. Today, Behcet's disease is recognised as a form of vasculitis, an inflammation of blood vessels that can affect almost any organ. It is one of the few diseases named after a Turkish doctor. The condition is most common along the ancient Silk Road, from the Mediterranean to East Asia, and Turkey has one of the highest rates in the world. Its exact cause is unknown, but researchers believe a combination of genetic factors and an unusual immune response, possibly triggered by infection, is involved. Symptoms tend to come and go, so diagnosis relies on recognising a pattern over time. Treatment aims to control inflammation and protect the eyes, since untreated eye involvement can lead to blindness.

paragraph_raw: Obstructive sleep apnoea is a common condition in which the muscles of the throat relax during sleep and the airway becomes partly or completely blocked. Breathing stops for ten seconds or longer, the level of oxygen in the blood falls, and the brain briefly wakes the person to restart breathing. This may happen dozens or even hundreds of times a night, usually without the person remembering it. Loud snoring with pauses and gasps is a typical sign, often noticed first by a partner. Because sleep is constantly interrupted, people feel exhausted during the day and may fall asleep while driving. Over years, the condition is linked to high blood pressure, heart disease and diabetes. Losing weight can help, and many patients use a machine that blows air through a mask to keep the airway open at night.

paragraph_raw: Gentrification describes what happens when wealthier residents move into a lower-income urban neighbourhood. Often it begins with artists and students attracted by low rents and old buildings with character. Cafes, galleries and restaurants follow, the area becomes fashionable, and property prices rise. Supporters point to the benefits: renovated buildings, safer streets, new businesses and more tax income for the city. Critics, however, focus on those who are pushed out. Long-term tenants, small shopkeepers and older residents may no longer be able to afford rents in the area where they have lived for decades, and the local community that made the neighbourhood attractive in the first place can disappear. Istanbul districts such as Cihangir and Karakoy have often been discussed as examples. Cities have tried various responses, including rent controls and requirements for affordable housing in new developments.

paragraph_raw: Few economic policies cause as much debate as the minimum wage. Traditional economic theory predicts that if the government forces wages above the level set by the market, employers will hire fewer workers, so some of the people the policy aims to help will lose their jobs. In 1994, however, the economists David Card and Alan Krueger compared fast-food restaurants in New Jersey, which had just raised its minimum wage, with those in neighbouring Pennsylvania, which had not. They found no fall in employment in New Jersey. Their study was hotly debated, and later research has produced mixed results. Many economists now believe that moderate increases have little effect on jobs, while very large increases may cause losses, especially in poorer regions. Card shared the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2021, partly for this work.

paragraph_raw: Most people are born with two kidneys but can live a healthy life with only one. paragraph_raw: A battery stores energy in chemical form and releases it as electricity. Inside every battery are two electrodes, separated by a material called an electrolyte. When the battery is connected to a device, a chemical reaction at one electrode releases electrons, which flow through the external circuit, powering the device, to the other electrode. Meanwhile, charged particles called ions move through the electrolyte inside the battery to balance the charge. In rechargeable lithium-ion batteries, used in phones and electric cars, applying electricity pushes the lithium ions back, resetting the battery. Over hundreds of cycles, small unwanted reactions gradually reduce how much energy a battery can hold.

paragraph_raw: Babies begin learning language long before they speak, by listening to the voices around them. To supply the growing capital, Roman and Byzantine engineers built one of the longest water systems of the ancient world, bringing water from springs in Thrace through hundreds of kilometres of channels, tunnels and bridges. Its most visible part in Istanbul today is the Valens Aqueduct, completed in the late fourth century. Its stone arches, nearly a kilometre long, still cross the valley between two of the city's hills, and modern traffic passes beneath them. Water reaching the city was stored in open reservoirs and underground cisterns, which allowed the city to survive long sieges. The Ottomans repaired the aqueduct and continued to use it, and the famous architect Sinan later built new water systems of his own.

paragraph_raw: In 1465, the Ottoman surgeon Serefeddin Sabuncuoglu, working in the city of Amasya, completed a surgical textbook called Cerrahiyetu'l-Haniye, or Imperial Surgery. Written in Turkish and presented to Sultan Mehmed II, it drew heavily on an earlier Arabic work by the Andalusian surgeon al-Zahrawi, but Sabuncuoglu added his own cases and, remarkably, colourful illustrations showing operations being performed. The pictures show surgical instruments, the position of patients and even the surgeon's hands at work. Unusually for the period, some illustrations depict female surgeons treating female patients. Historians of medicine value the book as one of the earliest illustrated surgical texts in the Islamic world. Only a few handwritten copies survive, kept in libraries in Istanbul and Paris, and Sabuncuoglu's name is now honoured by a medical history museum in Amasya.

paragraph_raw: Sepsis occurs when the body's response to an infection gets out of control and starts to damage its own tissues and organs. It can begin with something as ordinary as a urinary infection, pneumonia or an infected cut. Instead of fighting the infection locally, the immune system triggers widespread inflammation; blood pressure can fall, and organs such as the kidneys and lungs may begin to fail. Sepsis is a leading cause of death in hospitals worldwide, yet the early signs are easily missed because they resemble flu: fever or very low temperature, a fast heartbeat, rapid breathing, confusion and extreme weakness. Speed matters enormously. For patients in septic shock, every hour of delay in starting antibiotics has been linked with a higher risk of death. Health campaigns therefore urge people to ask a simple question when someone becomes suddenly and seriously unwell: 'Could it be sepsis?'

paragraph_raw: In 2018, researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology published one of the largest studies of how news spreads online. They analysed around 126,000 stories shared on Twitter by about three million people over more than ten years, and checked each story against the judgements of independent fact-checking organisations. The results were striking. False stories spread significantly farther, faster and more widely than true ones; true stories took about six times as long to reach 1,500 people. Surprisingly, automated accounts, or bots, spread true and false news at roughly the same rate, so the difference was mainly due to humans. The researchers suggested one reason: false stories tended to be more novel and surprising, and they provoked stronger emotions such as disgust and fear, which made people more eager to share them.

paragraph_raw: Occam's razor is a principle named after William of Ockham, an English friar and philosopher of the fourteenth century. In its popular form, it says that when there are competing explanations for something, the one that makes the fewest assumptions should usually be preferred. If you hear hoofbeats in a field in Turkey, for example, you should think of horses before zebras. Scientists often use the razor as a practical guide, because simpler theories are easier to test and less likely to contain hidden errors. However, the principle is a rule of thumb, not a law of nature. Sometimes the truth is complicated: quantum physics, for instance, is far stranger than earlier theories, yet it explains observations they could not. The razor tells us where to start looking, not where we must end up.

paragraph_raw: Before the Industrial Revolution, most peppered moths in England were pale with dark speckles, which hid them well on lichen-covered tree trunks. paragraph_raw: In parts of eastern North America, certain cicadas spend most of their lives underground as young insects, feeding on fluids from tree roots. Then, after exactly 13 or 17 years depending on the species, millions emerge almost at once, climb the trees, shed their skins and fill the air with deafening mating calls for a few weeks before dying. Scientists have long wondered why the cycles are 13 and 17, both prime numbers. One popular explanation is that a prime-numbered cycle rarely lines up with the shorter population cycles of predators, so no predator can time its own boom to match. Another advantage comes from sheer numbers: birds and other animals feast, but they cannot possibly eat them all. In 2024, two broods emerged together for the first time since 1803.

paragraph_raw: During a strong earthquake, some of the worst damage is caused not by the shaking itself but by the ground beneath buildings. In loose, sandy soil that is soaked with water, the shaking pushes the grains closer together and raises the pressure of the water between them. For a short time the grains lose contact with one another, and the soil behaves like a thick liquid. Heavy buildings can then tilt, sink or even topple over while remaining largely undamaged. In 1964, apartment blocks in Niigata, Japan, famously tipped onto their sides. In Turkey's 1999 Marmara earthquake, many buildings in Adapazari sank into the ground or leaned dangerously. Engineers now test soil before construction and can strengthen it, for example by compacting it or draining the water.

paragraph_raw: Before vaccines, polio paralysed thousands of children every year, and in the worst cases it stopped the muscles used for breathing. In 1928, two researchers in Boston, Philip Drinker and Louis Shaw, built a machine to keep such patients alive. The patient lay inside a large metal tank with only the head outside. paragraph_raw: Whooping cough, or pertussis, is a bacterial infection that starts like an ordinary cold. After a week or two, however, it causes violent coughing fits, often followed by a high-pitched 'whoop' as the patient struggles to breathe in. The cough can last for months, which is why it is called the hundred-day cough in some languages. In older children and adults it is exhausting but rarely dangerous. For young babies, though, it can be deadly, and they may not whoop at all; instead, they may briefly stop breathing. Since protection from the vaccine fades over the years, adults can catch the infection and pass it on without knowing. For this reason, many countries now offer the vaccine to pregnant women, whose antibodies cross the placenta and protect the baby in its first weeks.

paragraph_raw: In Constantinople, chariot races at the Hippodrome were followed with fierce passion, and fans belonged to rival groups known as the Blues and the Greens. paragraph_raw: For most of history, time was measured by the movement of the Earth, but our planet's spin is slightly irregular. Since 1967, the second has instead been defined by atoms: it is the time taken for a particular kind of radiation from caesium atoms to complete 9,192,631,770 cycles. Atomic clocks based on this principle would lose less than a second in millions of years. The newest optical clocks are so precise that they can detect the tiny difference in the flow of time between a shelf and the floor, because time passes slightly faster further from the Earth's gravity. Such clocks keep satellite navigation and financial networks synchronised.

paragraph_raw: When the heart's electrical rhythm suddenly becomes chaotic, it stops pumping blood effectively, and the person collapses. paragraph_raw: Radon is a radioactive gas produced naturally when uranium in soil and rocks breaks down. It has no colour, smell or taste, so people can be exposed for years without knowing. Fortunately, testing a home is simple and cheap, and high levels can usually be reduced by sealing cracks and improving ventilation.

paragraph_raw: In 1957, the Sydney Opera House was expected to open in 1963 at a cost of seven million Australian dollars. It opened in 1973, having cost over one hundred million. Such overruns are so common that the psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky gave the tendency a name: the planning fallacy. People estimate how long a task will take by imagining how it should go, rather than by remembering how similar tasks went. In one study, students predicted they would finish their theses in about a month, but on average took about 55 days. A useful remedy is to ask how long comparable projects actually took.

paragraph_raw: In 1959, the Soviet scientist Dmitry Belyaev began an unusual experiment on a fur farm in Siberia. paragraph_raw: Dyslexia is a learning difference that makes it hard to connect written letters with the sounds they represent. paragraph_raw: Hepatitis B is a virus that attacks the liver. Adults who catch it usually recover, but babies infected at birth, often from their mothers, have a much higher chance of carrying the virus for life. Taiwan, where the virus was common, began a national newborn vaccination programme in 1984. Within two decades, liver cancer among children and young adults there had fallen sharply, and many countries now give the first dose within a day of birth.

paragraph_raw: Most tsunamis are caused by earthquakes beneath the sea, which suddenly lift or drop a large area of the sea floor. paragraph_raw: Universal basic income is the idea that every adult should receive a regular payment from the state, with no conditions attached. Other trials, from Kenya to the United States, have produced mixed findings, and the debate continues.

paragraph_raw: More than a century ago, the French engineer Max Ringelmann asked men to pull on a rope, alone and in groups. paragraph_raw: Glaucoma is a group of eye diseases that damage the optic nerve, which carries signals from the eye to the brain. It is often linked to raised pressure inside the eye. The most common type develops so gradually that it causes no pain, and it first steals side vision, which people rarely notice because the brain fills in the gaps. paragraph_raw: In 1865, the English economist William Stanley Jevons noticed something puzzling. James Watt's improved steam engine used coal far more efficiently than earlier designs, so one might expect Britain to burn less coal. Instead, coal use soared. Because the engines were now cheaper to run, they became profitable in many more industries, and total demand grew. This effect, now called the Jevons paradox, still matters today. More efficient cars, lighting or computers can lower costs so much that people use them more, wiping out some or even all of the expected savings. For this reason, some experts argue that efficiency alone cannot be relied on to cut energy use.

paragraph_raw: In 1964, two radio astronomers at Bell Labs in New Jersey, Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, were troubled by a faint, steady hiss in their large horn-shaped antenna. It came from every direction, day and night. Suspecting a fault, they checked the wiring and even removed pigeons that had been nesting inside, cleaning out what they politely called white dielectric material. The noise remained. Meanwhile, physicists at nearby Princeton University had predicted that if the universe began in a hot, dense state, a faint glow of radiation should still fill space. After a phone call between the two groups, the mystery was solved: the hiss was that glow, the oldest light in the universe. Penzias and Wilson received the Nobel Prize in 1978 for a discovery they had at first mistaken for a nuisance.

paragraph_raw: Few diseases have carried as much fear and stigma as leprosy. For centuries, people with it were forced to live apart, sometimes on islands or in special colonies, and in medieval Europe some had to carry bells to warn others of their approach. In 1873, the Norwegian doctor Gerhard Armauer Hansen identified the bacterium that causes it, one of the first times a specific germ was linked to a human disease. Contrary to popular belief, leprosy is not easily spread, and most people are naturally resistant. The disfigurement often associated with it results largely from nerve damage, which causes people to lose feeling and injure themselves without noticing. Since the 1980s, a combination of antibiotics has been able to cure it, and millions of patients have been treated.

paragraph_raw: The word quarantine comes from the Italian quaranta giorni, meaning forty days. In 1377, during repeated outbreaks of plague, the port city of Ragusa, today's Dubrovnik, ordered that ships and travellers arriving from infected areas wait thirty days in isolation before entering the city. Venice later extended the period to forty days, and the longer term gave the practice its name. Why forty is unclear; it may have had religious significance, since forty days appears often in the Bible. Officials did not understand germs, but they had observed that disease seemed to arrive with people and goods. Later, cities built special isolation hospitals called lazarettos on islands near their ports. The same basic idea, separating people who may have been exposed until it is clear they are not ill, was used again during the COVID-19 pandemic.

paragraph_raw: After Columbus crossed the Atlantic in 1492, plants, animals and diseases began moving between the Americas and the rest of the world on a scale never seen before. Historians call this the Columbian Exchange. From the Americas came maize, potatoes, tomatoes, peppers and cocoa; from Europe, Africa and Asia went wheat, sugar cane, horses and cattle. The effects were enormous. The potato, which grows well in poor soil, helped populations in northern Europe expand, while maize became a staple in parts of Africa. Turkish cuisine, too, would look very different without tomatoes and peppers. But the exchange also had a terrible side: diseases such as smallpox, to which Native Americans had no immunity, killed a huge share of the population.

paragraph_raw: In a famous 1999 experiment, Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris asked people to watch a short video of students passing basketballs and to count the passes made by the team in white. paragraph_raw: After the nuclear accident at Chernobyl in 1986, around 350,000 people were moved out of the surrounding area, and an exclusion zone of about 2,600 square kilometres was created. Many expected it to become a lifeless wasteland. Instead, wildlife has flourished. Camera traps and surveys have recorded wolves, elk, wild boar, lynx and even brown bears, and the endangered Przewalski's horses released there in the 1990s have multiplied. paragraph_raw: In 1986, about 3.5 million people a year, mostly in Africa and Asia, suffered from Guinea worm disease. If it succeeds, Guinea worm will be the first human disease eradicated without a vaccine or drug.

topic: Medicine (The Rise and Fall of Lobotomy)
paragraph_raw: In 1935, the Portuguese neurologist Egas Moniz introduced an operation that cut connections in the front of the brain to treat severe mental illness. He reported that many patients became calmer, and in 1949 he received the Nobel Prize. In the United States, Walter Freeman developed a faster version, inserting an instrument through the eye socket, sometimes in under ten minutes and outside an operating room. Tens of thousands of Americans were lobotomised. Many patients were indeed calmer, but often because they had become passive and emotionally flat, and some never lived independently again. By the mid-1950s, the first effective psychiatric drugs offered an alternative, and the operation fell out of use. Today it is often cited as a warning about treatments adopted before their long-term effects are properly studied.

paragraph_raw: Imagine a radio station funded entirely by listeners' donations. Anyone can tune in, whether they pay or not. Each listener may reason that one small donation will make no difference, and that the station will survive anyway. If enough people think this way, it closes, and everyone loses something they valued. Economists call this the free rider problem. It appears whenever a benefit cannot easily be limited to those who pay for it, from street lighting to national defence, and even in group projects at school. Societies have developed several responses. Governments fund some services through compulsory taxes. Charities publish lists of donors or offer small gifts, and communities rely on social pressure, since few people like being seen as the one who did not contribute.

paragraph_raw: In the valley of the Orkhon River in present-day Mongolia stand stone monuments carved in the 730s for the Turkic ruler Bilge Kagan and his brother Kul Tigin. Their inscriptions are the oldest known long texts in a Turkic language. Written in a runic-looking alphabet, they speak directly to the people, recalling victories and defeats and warning against the 'sweet words and soft silk' of the Chinese, which had tempted earlier generations away from their own way of life. For centuries no one could read them. Explorers rediscovered them in 1889, and in 1893 the Danish linguist Vilhelm Thomsen deciphered the script, beginning with a few words such as 'Turk'. Today the stones are an important symbol of Turkic heritage, and phrases from them appear in Turkish school textbooks.

paragraph_raw: Red and green light-emitting diodes, or LEDs, were invented in the 1960s, but a bright blue one eluded scientists for three decades. paragraph_raw: Sharks are fish, dolphins are mammals, and the extinct ichthyosaurs were reptiles, yet all three evolved the same streamlined shape, with a pointed snout, a dorsal fin and a powerful tail. Biologists call this convergent evolution: unrelated species facing similar challenges arrive at similar solutions. The camera-like eye evolved separately in vertebrates and in octopuses. Interestingly, the octopus version is arguably better designed, because its nerve fibres run behind the light-sensitive cells rather than in front of them, so it has no blind spot. Convergence suggests that the laws of physics strongly limit the range of workable designs.

paragraph_raw: In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, hat makers in Europe and America often used a mercury solution to turn animal fur into felt. Working in poorly ventilated rooms, they breathed in mercury vapour for years. Many developed trembling hands, memory loss, extreme shyness and sudden bursts of anger. In the hat-making town of Danbury, Connecticut, the tremors were so common that locals called them the 'Danbury shakes'. The expression 'mad as a hatter' probably reflects this poisoning, although scholars still argue about whether Lewis Carroll's famous character was based on it. The United States did not ban mercury in hat-making until 1941.

paragraph_raw: In a 1999 study, American psychologists gave men and women with strong maths backgrounds a difficult maths test. When participants were told that the test usually showed differences between men and women, the women scored noticeably lower than the men. When they were told that it showed no such differences, the gap disappeared. Later studies suggest the effect may be smaller than first thought, but it remains widely discussed in education.

paragraph_raw: In 1950, during a lunchtime conversation about flying saucers, the physicist Enrico Fermi suddenly asked his colleagues, 'But where is everybody?' His reasoning was simple. paragraph_raw: Between 1856 and 1863, Gregor Mendel, a monk in the city of Brno, grew and studied about 28,000 pea plants in his monastery garden. He chose peas because they have clear, either-or features, such as purple or white flowers and smooth or wrinkled seeds. When he crossed purple-flowered plants with white-flowered ones, all the offspring had purple flowers. Yet when those offspring were bred together, white flowers reappeared in roughly one plant in four. Mendel concluded that each plant carries two units for every trait, one from each parent, and that one unit can hide the other without destroying it. He published his results in 1866, but they were largely ignored. Only in 1900 did three scientists, working separately, rediscover his paper and recognise it as the foundation of genetics.

paragraph_raw: Asbestos is a natural mineral made of tiny fibres. Because it does not burn and insulates well, it was used throughout the twentieth century in roofs, pipes, walls and car brakes, and was often praised as a 'magic mineral'. Its danger lies in the fibres. When asbestos is broken or worn, they float into the air, and if breathed in they can lodge in the lungs for life. Diseases such as mesothelioma, a cancer of the lining around the lungs, may appear twenty to fifty years after exposure, which helped delay action against the material. Many countries have now banned it; Turkey did so in 2010. However, it remains inside many older buildings, where it is mostly harmless unless disturbed. Experts therefore warn that demolition and earthquake debris can release fibres, and that workers clearing rubble need proper masks.

paragraph_raw: For centuries, sailors could work out how far north or south they were from the height of the Sun, but not how far east or west. In 1714, Parliament offered a huge prize for a practical solution. paragraph_raw: In 1836, Michael Faraday lined a room with metal foil and charged it with powerful electricity. Inside, his instruments detected no electric effect. When charge builds up on a closed metal shell, it spreads over the outer surface in a way that cancels the electric field inside. Such a shell is now called a Faraday cage, and it does not even need to be solid: a mesh works, provided its holes are much smaller than the waves it must block. This also explains why a car offers good protection from lightning: the current flows around the metal body, not, as many people believe, because the rubber tyres insulate it.

paragraph_raw: Earth's magnetic field is produced by molten iron swirling in the planet's outer core, thousands of kilometres beneath our feet. Surprisingly, it has not always pointed the same way. That could expose satellites and power grids to more radiation from space, but the fossil record shows no link between past reversals and mass extinctions.

paragraph_raw: In the early twentieth century, a disease called pellagra was killing thousands of people a year in the southern United States. paragraph_raw: A panic attack is a sudden wave of intense fear that usually peaks within ten minutes. The heart races, breathing becomes fast and shallow, and many people feel dizzy, shaky or sure that they are about to die. Not surprisingly, first attacks often send people to hospital emergency departments, convinced they are having a heart attack. Although extremely unpleasant, a panic attack is not physically harmful, though new chest pain should always be checked. The bigger problem is often what follows. Some people begin to avoid places where an attack once happened, such as buses or shops, and their world gradually shrinks. Psychological therapy, which teaches people to face these situations step by step, is highly effective.

paragraph_raw: Many people assume that the main danger of falling into cold water is hypothermia, the dangerous cooling of the body. paragraph_raw: In 1772, the mathematician Joseph-Louis Lagrange showed that in a system of two large bodies, such as the Sun and the Earth, there are five special points where a small object can stay in the same position relative to both. paragraph_raw: Early electronic computers relied on vacuum tubes, glass bulbs that acted as switches. They were large, consumed a great deal of power, gave off heat and frequently burned out; the ENIAC computer of 1945 contained about 17,500 of them. Shockley later founded his own company in California, but his difficult management style drove eight of his best employees to leave and start a rival firm, an event often seen as the birth of Silicon Valley. Today a single smartphone chip contains billions of transistors.

paragraph_raw: The Book of Dede Korkut is a collection of twelve stories from the Oghuz Turks, a people who lived in Central Asia and later moved into Anatolia and Azerbaijan. paragraph_raw: In a classic 1973 study, researchers chose preschool children who already enjoyed drawing. Some were told they would receive a special certificate for drawing; others were not, though a few received one by surprise. Two weeks later, when the children were given free time with the same materials, those who had drawn to earn the certificate spent noticeably less time drawing than the others. The finding has fuelled debate about sticker charts in classrooms and paying children for good grades.

paragraph_raw: Since it was first seen in 1996, a strange disease has killed most of the Tasmanian devils living in the wild. Devil facial tumour disease is one of the very few cancers known to spread from one animal to another. Devils often bite each other's faces while fighting over food or mates, and in doing so they transfer living cancer cells, which grow into large tumours around the mouth. Normally, an immune system would reject foreign cells, but Tasmanian devils have very little genetic variety, so the tumour cells look familiar enough to go unnoticed. To protect the species, healthy devils have been kept in captivity and released on an island free of the disease. Encouragingly, some wild populations now show signs of evolving resistance.

paragraph_raw: In the 1960s, the Aral Sea in Central Asia was one of the four largest lakes in the world, supporting a busy fishing industry. paragraph_raw: Before the 1790s, soldiers wounded in battle often lay where they fell until the fighting was over, sometimes for a day or more, and many died who could have been saved. Dominique-Jean Larrey, a French army surgeon who later served Napoleon, changed this. He designed light, horse-drawn carriages, which he called flying ambulances, to carry the wounded away while the battle was still going on. He is also credited with insisting that patients be treated in order of how serious their injuries were, not according to their rank, and he treated enemy soldiers too. This method of sorting patients became known as triage, from a French word meaning 'to sort'. Today, emergency departments and disaster teams around the world still use triage to decide who needs help first.

paragraph_raw: In 1577, the astronomer Taqi al-Din, known in Turkish as Takiyuddin, completed one of the most advanced observatories of its time in Istanbul, with the support of Sultan Murad III. paragraph_raw: In 1954, the Turkish-born psychologist Muzafer Sherif took twenty-two eleven-year-old boys to a summer camp in Oklahoma. The boys were split into two groups, which at first did not know about each other. When the groups were brought together for a series of competitions, such as tug-of-war and baseball, hostility quickly grew: they called each other names, burned each other's flag and raided each other's cabins. Simply letting the groups spend time together, at meals or films, did not help. What worked was giving them goals that neither group could achieve alone, such as repairing the camp's water supply or pulling a broken-down truck. After several such tasks, friendships formed across group lines. Sherif concluded that conflict often grows out of competition for limited rewards, and cooperation on shared goals can reduce it.

paragraph_raw: In a famous 1978 study, psychologists interviewed recent lottery winners and found that, after some time had passed, they were not much happier than people who had won nothing. They also took less pleasure in everyday activities such as chatting with friends. This tendency to adapt to good fortune, returning to roughly our usual level of happiness, is called the hedonic treadmill: we keep running towards the next reward, yet stay in the same place. Later research showed that adaptation is not always complete; long-term unemployment, for example, can lower happiness for years. Still, the idea helps explain why a new car or phone thrills us only briefly.

paragraph_raw: Carbon capture aims to stop carbon dioxide from reaching the atmosphere, or to remove it once it is there. Some systems trap the gas from the chimneys of power plants and factories; others, called direct air capture, pull it straight out of ordinary air. The captured gas can be pumped deep underground. Since 1996, a Norwegian gas field has stored about a million tonnes a year beneath the North Sea, and in Iceland, carbon dioxide dissolved in water is injected into volcanic rock, where it turns to stone within two years. Yet the scale is tiny compared with the more than 35 billion tonnes humans release each year, and the technology is expensive and uses a lot of energy. Supporters see it as essential for industries that are hard to clean up; critics fear it gives polluters an excuse to delay cutting emissions.

paragraph_raw: The oldest known pieces of Earth are not great slabs of rock but tiny crystals of a mineral called zircon, some no wider than a human hair. Found in the Jack Hills of Western Australia, the oldest have been dated to about 4.4 billion years ago, only around 150 million years after our planet formed. Zircon is ideal for this work. It is extremely tough, surviving erosion and even being recycled into new rocks, and when it forms it traps uranium, which decays into lead at a precisely known rate, acting like a natural clock. paragraph_raw: Intermittent fasting has become one of the most popular diets of recent years. paragraph_raw: On Earth, every step we take puts weight on our bones, and that stress keeps them strong. In the weightlessness of space, the stress disappears, and astronauts can lose 1 to 1.5 per cent of the bone mass in their hips and spine every month, roughly what an older person with osteoporosis might lose in a year. Their muscles weaken too. To fight this, crew members on the International Space Station exercise for about two hours a day, running on a treadmill while held down by elastic straps and lifting against a special resistance machine. Even so, some lost bone may take years to return after landing, and some may never fully recover. This is a serious concern for planned missions to Mars, which could last more than two years. paragraph_raw: In 1751, the French writer Denis Diderot and the mathematician Jean d'Alembert published the first volume of the Encyclopedie, an enormous project that aimed to gather all human knowledge. paragraph_raw: During the First World War, thousands of soldiers developed strange symptoms: uncontrollable shaking, paralysis, loss of speech and terrible nightmares. paragraph_raw: The body mass index, or BMI, is calculated by dividing a person's weight in kilograms by the square of their height in metres. paragraph_raw: In a famous 1961 experiment, the psychologist Albert Bandura showed young children an adult playing with a large inflatable doll called Bobo. For some children, the adult attacked the doll, hitting it with a mallet, kicking it and shouting phrases such as 'Sock him in the nose!' Others saw an adult who played quietly. Later, each child was left alone in a room with toys, including a Bobo doll. Children who had watched the aggressive adult were far more likely to attack the doll, often copying the exact actions and words. Bandura argued that children learn not only through rewards and punishments, but also simply by watching others. Critics have pointed out that Bobo is designed to be punched and bounce back, so hitting it may be play rather than true aggression, but the study remains central to debates about violent media.

paragraph_raw: Hasankeyf, an ancient town on the River Tigris in south-eastern Turkey, had been inhabited for thousands of years. topic: History (The Universal Declaration of Human Rights)
paragraph_raw: After the horrors of the Second World War, the newly founded United Nations set out to define rights that every person should have, regardless of nationality, religion or wealth. A committee chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt, the widow of the American president, brought together experts from countries including China, France and Lebanon, who often disagreed about the philosophical basis of rights. On 10 December 1948, in Paris, the General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, with 48 countries in favour, none against and eight abstaining. The declaration was not a legally binding treaty, but it inspired many later agreements and national constitutions. It has been translated into more than 500 languages, more than any other document, and 10 December is now celebrated each year as Human Rights Day.

paragraph_raw: Where did the Moon come from? For centuries, nobody had a convincing answer. paragraph_raw: In 2015, a team of 270 researchers tried to repeat 100 psychology experiments that had been published in leading journals. Although almost all the original studies had reported significant results, only about a third of the repeat attempts did. The project helped spark what became known as the replication crisis. Part of the problem lay in how research was rewarded: journals preferred surprising, positive findings, so studies that found nothing often went unpublished, and researchers could try many analyses until one produced an eye-catching result. Psychology was not alone; similar problems were found in medicine and economics. In response, many scientists now publicly register their plans before collecting data and share their raw data, so others can check their work. paragraph_raw: In April 1815, Mount Tambora in Indonesia erupted in the largest volcanic explosion in recorded history, killing tens of thousands of people nearby. It threw huge amounts of sulphur gas high into the atmosphere, where it formed a thin veil that reflected sunlight. The following year, 1816, became known in Europe and North America as 'the year without a summer'. Snow fell in New England in June, crops failed, and food prices soared, leading to hunger and riots. Some historians link the haze to the fiery sunsets in paintings of the time, and the gloomy weather even to Mary Shelley's Frankenstein, begun that rainy summer by Lake Geneva.

paragraph_raw: Contact tracing is one of the oldest tools in public health. When someone is diagnosed with an infectious disease, trained workers ask whom they have been close to, then find those people, warn them and, if needed, test or isolate them. The method helped eradicate smallpox: rather than vaccinating everyone, teams vaccinated the contacts of each case, building a ring of immunity around it. It works best when a disease spreads slowly and when people trust the authorities enough to answer honestly. During the COVID-19 pandemic, many countries tried smartphone apps to do the job automatically, with mixed results, partly because of concerns about privacy.

paragraph_raw: In 1974, the economist Richard Easterlin noticed something puzzling. Within a country, richer people reported being happier than poorer ones. Yet as whole countries grew richer over the decades, average happiness barely changed. In the United States, incomes had risen sharply since the 1940s, but people said they were no happier. Later economists, using larger data sets, have argued that happiness does rise with income after all, just more slowly than expected, and the debate continues.

paragraph_raw: When enough people in a community are immune to an infectious disease, either through vaccination or past infection, the disease struggles to spread, because each infected person meets too few people who can catch it. This indirect protection, called herd immunity, shields those who cannot be vaccinated, such as newborn babies and people with weak immune systems. The share of people who need to be immune depends on how contagious the disease is. For measles, one of the most contagious diseases known, it is about 95 per cent; for polio, roughly 80 per cent. This is why even a small fall in vaccination rates can allow measles outbreaks to return, while seeming to make little difference for other diseases. Relying on natural infection to reach herd immunity, meanwhile, would cost many lives along the way.

paragraph_raw: Electronic cigarettes heat a liquid, usually containing nicotine and flavourings, into an aerosol that users breathe in. paragraph_raw: Between 1845 and 1852, Ireland suffered one of the worst famines in modern European history. Yet during the famine years, Ireland continued to export large quantities of grain and cattle to Britain, and the British government's relief efforts were limited and slow. Partly because emigration continued for decades, the island's population, around 8.5 million before the famine, is still lower today.

paragraph_raw: In 1959, at the height of the Cold War, twelve countries, including both the United States and the Soviet Union, signed a treaty about the one continent with no native population: Antarctica. The Antarctic Treaty declared that the continent should be used only for peaceful purposes. Military bases and weapons tests were banned, and nuclear explosions and the dumping of radioactive waste were forbidden. Countries agreed to set aside, without giving them up, their competing claims to territory, and scientists were to share their findings freely. Any member could inspect the research stations of others at any time. A later agreement, signed in 1991, banned mining, a ban that cannot easily be reviewed before 2048. Today more than fifty countries have joined, including Turkey in 1996, and the treaty is often cited as proof that rivals can cooperate when the stakes are clear.

paragraph_raw: On 27 August 1883, the volcanic island of Krakatoa, between Java and Sumatra, exploded with a force far greater than the largest nuclear weapon ever tested. paragraph_raw: During the Second World War, the German military encrypted its messages with Enigma machines, which scrambled each letter through a series of rotating wheels. The settings changed every day, giving around 158 million million million possible combinations, so the Germans believed the code was unbreakable. The first breakthrough, however, came from Polish mathematicians, including Marian Rejewski, who reconstructed the machine in the early 1930s and shared their work with Britain and France shortly before the war. At Bletchley Park in England, Alan Turing and others built electromechanical machines called 'bombes' to test possible settings quickly. They exploited German habits, such as starting messages with predictable phrases like weather reports. Historians estimate that the intelligence gained may have shortened the war by up to two years, though such figures are hard to prove.

paragraph_raw: Almost everyone sleeps badly sometimes, but for about one adult in ten, insomnia becomes a long-term problem, lasting for months. Many reach for sleeping pills, which can help for a short time but often lose their effect and may cause drowsiness the next day. Medical guidelines in many countries now recommend a different first treatment: cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, or CBT-I. Surprisingly, one of its key techniques is to spend less time in bed. Patients go to bed only when sleepy and get up at the same time every day, even after a bad night, so that the pressure to sleep builds up. They also learn to leave the bedroom if they lie awake, so the bed becomes linked with sleep rather than worry. The first weeks can be tiring, but the improvements tend to last far longer than those from pills.

paragraph_raw: Stuttering, in which the flow of speech is broken by repeated sounds, stretched sounds or silent blocks, affects around one per cent of adults and many more young children, most of whom grow out of it. For centuries it was blamed on nervousness, bad parenting or even the shape of the tongue, and some nineteenth-century surgeons cut patients' tongue muscles in an attempt to cure it. Research now shows that stuttering has strong genetic and neurological roots; brain scans reveal differences in the areas that plan and time speech. Anxiety does not cause stuttering, though it can make it worse. Many people who stutter speak fluently when singing or talking in unison with others, which suggests the problem lies in starting and timing speech rather than in knowing what to say. Speech therapy can help, and many famous actors, politicians and writers have stuttered.

paragraph_raw: Lake Van in eastern Turkey is so salty and alkaline that only one fish species is known to live in it: the pearl mullet, or inci kefali. Every spring, from April to June, huge numbers of these fish leave the lake and swim up the freshwater rivers that feed it to lay their eggs, leaping up small waterfalls. Fishing bans in the breeding season, along with fish passes built over river barriers, have helped the population recover, and the migration has become a popular sight for visitors.

paragraph_raw: You might expect the first digits of numbers in real-life data to be spread evenly from 1 to 9. paragraph_raw: During the twentieth century, average scores on IQ tests rose steadily in many countries, by roughly three points every decade. paragraph_raw: Chemotherapy has an unexpected origin. During both world wars, doctors noticed that soldiers exposed to mustard gas had very low numbers of white blood cells. In the early 1940s, the pharmacologists Louis Goodman and Alfred Gilman at Yale wondered whether a related chemical could attack cancers of the white blood cells. In 1942, they treated a patient with advanced lymphoma, and his tumours shrank dramatically, though the cancer later returned. The work was kept secret during the war and published in 1946. It offered early proof that a drug could shrink a cancer, and it opened the way for the many chemotherapy drugs used today.

paragraph_raw: The polygraph, often called a lie detector, was developed in the early 1920s. It records changes in breathing, heart rate, blood pressure and sweating while a person answers questions, on the assumption that lying causes stress. For these reasons, scientists have criticised the polygraph, and courts in many countries do not accept its results as evidence, although some employers and police forces still use it.

paragraph_raw: Mary Anning was born in 1799 in Lyme Regis, a small town on the south coast of England whose crumbling cliffs are full of fossils. Her family was poor, and she sold fossils to tourists to make a living. When she was about twelve, she and her brother uncovered the first complete skeleton of an ichthyosaur, a dolphin-like marine reptile, to be recognised by scientists. She later found the first nearly complete plesiosaur, a strange animal with a tiny head and a long neck, so unusual that the famous French scientist Georges Cuvier at first suspected it was a fake. Despite her expertise, as a woman she could not join the Geological Society of London, and male scientists often published her discoveries without mentioning her name. Today she is recognised as one of the most important fossil hunters in history.

paragraph_raw: Every second, around 60 billion tiny particles called neutrinos pass through each square centimetre of your body, most of them produced by nuclear reactions in the Sun. You feel nothing, because neutrinos have almost no mass and no electric charge, and they hardly ever interact with matter; many could pass through a light-year of solid lead without stopping. Their existence was proposed in 1930 by Wolfgang Pauli to explain missing energy in radioactive decay, but they were not detected until 1956. To catch the rare collisions, scientists build huge detectors deep underground, shielded from other radiation. One, IceCube, uses a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice. Studying neutrinos helps scientists look deep inside the Sun and exploding stars, places from which light cannot escape directly.

paragraph_raw: When AIDS was first identified in 1981, a diagnosis was effectively a death sentence. The virus that causes it, HIV, attacks the immune system, leaving the body unable to fight infections. Then, in 1996, doctors began combining several antiretroviral drugs at once. Because the virus mutates quickly, it could resist one drug, but rarely three together. Deaths in wealthy countries fell dramatically within a few years. Just as importantly, studies have shown that when treatment reduces the virus in the blood to undetectable levels, it cannot be passed on through sex, a finding summarised as 'undetectable equals untransmittable'. The main challenges now are reaching everyone who needs testing and treatment, and the stigma that still stops many people from seeking help.

paragraph_raw: Erythropoietin, or EPO, is a hormone made by the kidneys that tells the body to produce more red blood cells, which carry oxygen to the muscles. A urine test was introduced in 2000, and later the 'biological passport', which tracks an athlete's blood over time, made cheating far harder, though not impossible.

paragraph_raw: Why does rubbing a bumped knee make it hurt less? In 1965, the scientists Ronald Melzack and Patrick Wall proposed an answer known as the gate control theory. They suggested that nerve signals from touch and pressure can partly 'close a gate' in the spinal cord, reducing the pain signals that reach the brain. The theory also helped explain why emotions and attention affect pain, since the brain can send signals down to the gate. It led to treatments such as TENS machines, which use mild electrical pulses on the skin to ease pain.

paragraph_raw: The Piraha are a small group of a few hundred people living along a river in the Amazon rainforest of Brazil. Their language has fascinated and divided linguists. According to the American researcher Daniel Everett, who lived among them for many years, Piraha has no words for exact numbers, not even 'one' or 'two', only terms meaning something like 'a small amount' and 'a larger amount'. Experiments found that speakers struggled to match exact quantities of more than three objects. Everett also claimed the language lacks recursion, the ability to place one phrase inside another, which some famous linguists consider a universal feature of human language. His claims sparked a fierce debate that continues today, partly because very few outsiders speak Piraha well enough to check them.

paragraph_raw: Unlike the vaccines for measles or polio, which protect for many years, the flu vaccine has to be updated and taken again every year. Because vaccines take months to produce, the choice must be made early, and when the prediction is wrong, the vaccine works less well.

paragraph_raw: The Caesarean section, in which a baby is delivered through a cut in the mother's abdomen, is now one of the most common operations in the world. paragraph_raw: People often say 'I'm so OCD' when they mean they like a tidy desk, but obsessive-compulsive disorder is far more serious. It affects around one to two per cent of people and involves two linked parts. Obsessions are unwanted, distressing thoughts that keep returning, such as fears of contamination or of causing harm. Compulsions are repeated actions, like washing hands or checking locks, performed to reduce the anxiety. The relief is only temporary, so the cycle repeats and can take up hours each day. Most people with OCD know their fears are unrealistic, which makes the condition especially frustrating. The most effective treatment is a form of therapy called exposure and response prevention, in which patients gradually face their fears without performing the compulsion, sometimes combined with medication.

topic: Sport (Pierre de Coubertin and the Modern Olympics)
paragraph_raw: The ancient Olympic Games were held at Olympia in Greece for over a thousand years before ending in the late fourth century. In the 1880s, a French aristocrat, Pierre de Coubertin, became convinced that sport could build character and bring nations together, and he campaigned to revive the Games. In 1894 he founded the International Olympic Committee in Paris, and two years later the first modern Olympics were held in Athens, with around 240 athletes from fourteen countries, all of them men. Coubertin wanted the Games to move between cities, and he designed the five interlocking rings in 1913, representing the continents that would take part. Yet he opposed women competing, calling it 'impractical, uninteresting' and improper. Today, women make up about half of all Olympic athletes.

paragraph_raw: Basque, spoken by around 750,000 people in northern Spain and south-western France, is a linguistic puzzle. Most languages in Europe belong to the Indo-European family, which includes English, Spanish, Russian and Hindi, but Basque is related to no other living language. Many linguists think it is a survivor from before the Indo-European languages arrived in Europe several thousand years ago. Its grammar is very different from its neighbours: verbs change to show both the subject and the object, and a special ending marks who performed an action. Under the dictatorship of Francisco Franco, from 1939 to 1975, public use of Basque was severely restricted. Since then, schools teaching in Basque have helped the number of speakers grow, an unusual success story for a minority language.
